Stéphanie in the streets of Montréal.
Très impliquée dans le milieu communauta: Deeply involved in the community scene in Montréal-Nord and surrounding areas, Stéphanie Germain divides her time between her roles as a community organizer and as executive director of Éduconnexion, a non-profit organization that promotes education and civic participation among young people.
Aujourd’hui, elle retire ses nombreux ch: Today, she takes off her many hats and opens up to La Converse in an honest conversation.
Stéphanie arrive de manière chaleureuse: Stéphanie arrives warmly in the early evening. As usual, she is polished and put together. “I love fashion,” she tells me, laughing. “My favourite way to communicate is through the way I dress.” Always at ease, always stylish: that is probably the best way to describe Stéphanie's appearance. “The time I spend getting ready, taking care of my skin while playing music… it's often my favourite part of my whole evening,” she says with a laugh.
Une fois bien installée, elle entame un: Once she is settled in, she begins a unique story: her own. “I arrived in Quebec in the middle of February. I still remember my first contact with the cold and the snow: I had barely stepped off the plane when I lost my shoe, and my foot touched the cold ground,” Stéphanie begins, her gaze far away, lost in her memories. “It was a bit like I was Cinderella,” she adds, laughing.
Ayant grandi dans les HLM de Montréal-No: Having grown up in the public housing projects of Montréal-Nord, Stéphanie Germain wants to represent hope for the young people of her neighbourhood. With a great deal of emotion, she shares with us her journey and the ambitions that led her to where she is today. “What motivated me were really the memories of my childhood in Montréal-Nord… A big part of my story is in that neighbourhood,” she tells us, recalling memories she visibly cherishes. Remembering the genesis of her social engagement always fills her with a sense of nostalgia.
« Il m’arrive de penser à tous les progr: “Sometimes I think about all the programs I didn't have access to when I was a teenager. Today, those are the opportunities I want to offer to these young people,” she continues. After a moment of reflection, the community organizer adds that “the experiences [she] didn't have when [she] was younger [pushed her] to create activities by, for and with young people so that they benefit from them, but also give back to the community.”
Stéphanie a découvert le milieu communau: Stéphanie discovered the community sector through several initiatives. “I started by teaching dance classes in community centres,” she says. “I've always loved dancing. Being able to teach it to younger kids allowed me to combine two things I love.”
Arrivée à l’âge adulte, elle se découvre: As a young adult, she discovered a certain talent for the stage. “I had started getting on stage much more often, hosting galas in Montréal-Nord back then,” she recalls.
Tout indiquait qu’elle avait un avenir t: Everything indicated that she had a future mapped out in hosting. Studies in communications and media had introduced her to that specialization, but it was by happening into a role as an activity leader at Louis-Joseph-Papineau secondary school, in the Saint-Michel neighbourhood, that she began working with young people every day. “At the time, I saw that a position was available, so I applied without asking too many questions. It spoke to me and that was enough for me,” she sums up.
« Je me suis formée sur le terrain », dé: “I trained on the ground,” she says. The director of Éduconnexion has spent a great deal of time with young people and families. “I sit down with myself and I ask: what could I create? What would I have liked to have when I was younger?”
Une très jeune Stéphanie Germain. Courto: A very young Stéphanie Germain. Courtesy of Stéphanie Germain.
Aujourd’hui, Stéphanie enchaîne les orga: Today, Stéphanie organizes one event after another by and for young people. She holds an important place not only in Montréal-Nord, but also in the lives of hundreds of young people to whom she has offered mentorship and inclusive community activities. “It's so important to know that when you get up in the morning and something is wrong in your community, you have the power to change it,” she adds. That power to act takes many forms: “writing letters to elected officials, mobilizing political leaders, going to knock on the door of city hall, for example,” she lists.
La route n’est pas toujours facile, et S: The road is not always easy, and Stéphanie can attest to that. As she recounts her journey, marked by the everyday ups and downs, she says she went through a major change after the death of George Floyd in the United States in 2020. “After George Floyd's tragic death, there was a kind of shift. From that moment on, it became like a very intense race. All the attention was turned to the issues facing the different Black communities,” she says.
« Je me suis sentie essoufflée à parler: “I felt out of breath from talking about these traumas, about the things we live through as Black people on Quebec and Canadian soil,” she explains. Stéphanie describes how she had to share everything and pour everything out from her heart in a very short span of time. She also adds that her fatigue, caused by the accumulation of activities related to her commitment to fighting anti-Black racism, pushed her to isolate herself. “I had to close myself off from others. I shut down my social media, and I limited the access people could have to me.”
Stéphanie remarque toutefois qu’elle a e: Stéphanie notes, however, that she has been very lucky. She is grateful for everything her work has brought her. “I didn't pay the price of my life to assert my intentions,” she says. “There are people like Fredy Villanueva who gave their lives for this cause. I also think of <l1>Jayson Colin and other young people who lost their lives because society failed to protect them</l1>,” she declares in a strong voice.
Fredy Villanueva, qui était un ami de St: Fredy Villanueva, who was a friend of Stéphanie's, was murdered during a police intervention in 2008. Fredy's story, besides shaking all of Montréal, was particularly hard on Stéphanie. She still remembers the times when his family invited her to spend afternoons at their home, or the barbecues she attended with the Villanuevas. “Some people were shocked by Fredy's tragic end without even knowing him. So, for me, there's no need to say how hard it was,” she says, lost in her memories.
« On a vu beaucoup de jeunes de nos comm: “We've seen a lot of young people from our communities, especially young Black and Arab people, die like that. To me, that says a lot about the responsibility our society has toward our youth,” she hammers home. If society failed to protect these young people, the answer to that failure lies in how we conceive of the problem: “Gun violence, no matter what form it takes, must be considered a public health and safety issue,” she believes. In other words, she continues, we need to offer local services for young people and families, who are the first to suffer from this violence.
« On doit s’assurer de prendre soin de n: “We have to make sure we take care of our young people,” Stéphanie stresses. That is why, over the years, the community organizer has committed to setting up a large number of projects dedicated to youth. “We owe them at least that,” she says.
<strong>Être Noire et grandir au Québec<: Being Black and growing up in Quebec
Stéphanie se remémore sa propre adolesce: Stéphanie looks back on her own adolescence as a young Black girl in Montréal. Her “period of awakening,” as she calls it, came in the middle of high school. “At 14, when you're a young Black girl in Montréal, you don't learn much about your people. You ask yourself questions, you don't know much about yourself or about the world,” she says dejectedly.
L’histoire des Noirs est peu ou pas ense: Black history is little taught, if at all, in Quebec. According to the Montréal native, this has contributed greatly to the isolation and alienation of Black people, especially young people. “There was very little talk about the presence of Black peoples in Canada. There were forced displacements of our communities,” she begins by explaining. She says she would have liked to learn more about her community's ancestors, and that it is necessary to teach history to young Black people in Quebec. “When we think about Black history, it's also the history of the country. I think it would have been necessary to show us how we were actors in history, how we contributed at every level to building this country,” she says.
C’est d’ailleurs un peu ce qu’elle fait: That is, in fact, somewhat what she does today in the mentorship activities she has set up. Stéphanie Germain works with people like <l1>Svens Télémaque</l1> and Webster (Aly Ndiaye), who tell the story of Black people in Canada.
Stéphanie se remémore le discours d’un p: Stéphanie recalls a pastor's speech she heard at a funeral. “He said that when someone dies close to us, our first reflex is to question our own death, our own existence. He asked us to think about what we wanted to leave on Earth after our death,” she recounts thoughtfully. Even today, those words echo in the young woman's mind.
Cela va au-delà de sa personne et de ses: It goes beyond her as a person and her actions, she thinks. “One day, when I'm no longer here, what will I have left to young people and to future generations of young people? What I'm building today is exactly for them,” she explains.
Stéphanie est néanmoins consciente de so: Stéphanie is nonetheless aware of her privilege: that of being able to contribute to the life of the community. She hopes that young people themselves will be able to give back to generations to come. “I'm in a spirit of sharing, a spirit of ‘giving back,’” she says. “And I want others to be in that spirit too.”
Ce que Stéphanie souhaite pour la jeunes: What Stéphanie wishes for youth is to act, act and act. She has this message for young people from the neighbourhoods: “Rest assured that if you speak up, there will be people to hear you. Never be afraid to speak, and know that you deserve all the attention.”
« Miss Nana Germain » croit fortement en: “Miss Nana Germain” strongly believes in young people's civic engagement. “Use your genius, be courageous. Tell people you're here, that you exist and that you have the right to contribute to the change you want to see and want to create.”
« Ce n’est pas seulement mon travail, c’: “It's not just my work, it's also my life, really,” she concludes on a strong note.
